summary: Robust Header Compression (ROHC) shrinks packet headers on links where bandwidth is precious. The profiles in RFC 3095 assume the link never reorders packets. This memo discusses what changes when the channel can reorder packets, gives guidance for running the existing profiles over such channels, and offers suggestions for designing new profiles.

eli5.summary: Packet headers are like long address labels on small parcels. Squashing the labels saves space, but only works if parcels arrive in order. This memo explains what to do when the parcels get shuffled on the way.

subtitle: How header compression built for in-order links can cope when packets arrive shuffled.

tldr.problem: The ROHC profiles in RFC 3095 assume the channel between compressor and decompressor keeps packets in order, and its wording led some to conclude ROHC cannot work over channels that reorder packets.
tldr.mechanism: This memo explains where reordering hurts (the LSB interpretation interval, R-mode references, mode transitions) and gives guidance: send more sequence number bits, delay shrinking the reference window, prefer U/O-mode, and adjust the interval offset p in new profiles.
tldr.outcome: It is informational and specifies no new technology. It shows that existing profiles can be implemented to tolerate reordering, at some cost in compression efficiency.

today: RFC 4224 is an Informational memo with no recorded obsoleting or updating RFC. It specifies no new technology and offers guidance for implementers of the RFC 3095 profiles and designers of new profiles.

sections.title: Why Reordering Matters to ROHC
sections.content:
RObust Header Compression (ROHC), defined in RFC 3095, is a framework for header compression with a set of compression profiles. One operating assumption of those profiles is that the channel between compressor and decompressor keeps packets in order for each compressed flow. That assumption fitted the channels considered at the time, and it let the designers focus on compression efficiency and tolerance to packet loss.

Since 2001 people have asked whether ROHC works over channels that do not guarantee in-order delivery. The memo says the claim that it cannot is a misconception, though the wording of RFC 3095 invites it. It discusses how to implement the existing profiles over such channels, either by making compressors use sufficiently robust compressed headers, by modifying decompressors to tolerate reordered packets, or both.

Cases where an external sequence number can detect reordering, such as compression over an IPsec ESP tunnel, are explicitly out of scope.
sections.eli5: Header compression was designed for roads where cars never overtake each other. People asked what happens when they do, and this memo answers.

sections.title: Which Profiles Are Covered
sections.content:
In this memo "ROHC" means profiles 0x0001, 0x0002 and 0x0003 from RFC 3095, profile 0x0004 for IP-only headers, and profiles 0x0007 and 0x0008 for UDP-Lite. Profile 0x0000 (uncompressed) is not affected by reordering. The Link-Layer Assisted profiles 0x0005 and 0x0105 need in-order delivery as a fundamental requirement, so they cannot be used over reordering channels and the memo does not apply to them.

Profiles 0x0002, 0x0004 and 0x0008 need special care. Their sequence number (SN) is generated at the compressor, and the LSB interpretation interval offset is always p = -1. The SN must therefore increase for every packet received, which means reordered packets cannot be decompressed unless the profile is revised.

The memo considers single-hop channels, such as a wireless link with retransmissions or bicasting during handoff, and multi-hop virtual channels such as IP tunnels.
sections.eli5: Some versions of the squashing scheme can cope with shuffling and some cannot. The memo says which is which.

sections.title: Where Reordering Causes Trouble
sections.content:
ROHC encodes the sequence number with LSB encoding: only the least significant bits are sent, and the decompressor reads them against an interpretation interval around a reference value. The offset p sets how far below the reference a value may fall, which is how many packets can arrive late. The rest of the interval covers losses, so raising p for reordering lowers the loss tolerance.

For profiles 0x0001, 0x0003 and 0x0007, p is 1 when 4 or fewer SN bits are sent, and grows with the number of bits. Sending 8 SN bits gives p = 7. A packet carrying only 4 or 6 SN bits tolerates being just one packet out of sequence. For the other profiles p = -1, so no late packet can be decompressed.

In R-mode, the compressor only uses references the decompressor has acknowledged. A late updating packet can set the decompressor's reference to a value the compressor has already dropped from its window (the "missing reference" problem), so the two lose synchronization. A late non-updating packet (R-0 or R-1*) can be decompressed against the wrong reference, and because these packets carry no verification, a wrongly decompressed packet can reach the upper layers.

In U/O-mode every packet type updates the context and is verified, so failures caused by reordering can be detected. The memo therefore says U/O-mode should be preferred on channels known to reorder packets. Reordering on the feedback channel has no impact in either mode.
sections.eli5: The decompressor guesses the full label from a few clues and a recent reference. If a late parcel shows up after the reference has moved on, the guess can be wrong.

sections.title: Consequences and Side Effects
sections.content:
The memo lists four effects. One optional function, ROHC segmentation, cannot work at all: segments carry no sequencing information, so a segmented packet with a segment out of order cannot be decompressed and is discarded. Segmentation should not be used where reordering can occur. This is local to the compressor.

Reordering also raises the chance of context damage, where a late change or updating packet changes the decompressor context in a way the compressor does not expect. It increases decompression failures that can be detected (U/O and R-mode) and, in R-mode only, failures that cannot be detected for R-0 and R-1* packets.

Mode transitions are exposed too. If a UO-0 packet is delayed by at least one round-trip time while the decompressor switches to R-mode, the late packet may be treated as an R-0 packet, decompressed wrongly and forwarded. The memo says transitions from U/O-mode to R-mode should be avoided when reordering can occur.

For list compression, encoding type 0 does not use reference lists and is preferred over reordering channels.
sections.eli5: When parcels get shuffled, some labels get misread, a few of them silently. The safest choice is the scheme that double-checks every label.

sections.title: Making ROHC Tolerant of Reordering
sections.content:
Compressor-side methods need no change to the specifications or to the decompressor. A compressor can repeat each context update more times in the optimistic approach. In R-mode it can delay advancing its sliding window until no acknowledgement for the values it would discard can still arrive, based on the maximum delay reordering can add. It can also choose packet types that send more SN bits, for example UOR-2*-ext0 in place of UO-0. The price is that such a compressor always sends at least 3 octets in R-mode or 4 octets in U/O-mode, compared with 1 octet for an aggressive implementation on an in-order channel. These methods should not be used when reordering is known not to occur.

Decompressor-side methods include reducing feedback when many UOR-2 packets with extensions arrive, not acknowledging a packet that is identifiably sequentially late, and, after a failed decompression, retrying backward in the interpretation interval as opposed to forward.

For profile design, new revisions of profiles 0x0002, 0x0004 and 0x0008 should use the p algorithm of profile 0x0001 instead of p = -1. Setting p near 2^k / 2 makes reordering and loss tolerance equal. The memo's example, keeping loss robustness a priority, uses about twice as much positive range as negative, giving p = 2^k / 3.
sections.eli5: You can send longer labels so late parcels are still readable, or keep old references a bit longer. Both cost a little space, so only do it when parcels really get shuffled.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it adds no security risks beyond those of RFC 3095. It adds that the approach may lower risks related to context damage in R-mode with injected packets, when sequentially late packets do not update the context.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about, and one kind of trick gets a bit harder.
